Criticism of the presidential electoral voting system often centers on a basic question of democratic fairness: should the candidate with the most votes nationwide always win? In systems where presidents are chosen through electoral votes assigned by states or regions rather than by a direct national popular vote, many people argue that the answer is yes. They see the current arrangement as an indirect method that can weaken the principle of political equality.

One major criticism is that not all votes carry the same practical weight. Because electoral votes are distributed by state and most states award all of them to the candidate who wins that state, a small shift in one competitive state can matter far more than a large number of votes in a state that is safely controlled by one party. As a result, candidates often focus their time, money, and policy promises on a limited number of closely contested states while paying much less attention to the rest of the country. Critics argue that this encourages a narrow campaign strategy instead of a truly national one.

Another common objection is that the system can produce a winner who did not receive the most votes from the public as a whole. Even if this does not happen often, opponents say the possibility itself is troubling. They believe it can damage trust in elections by making citizens feel that the final result does not reflect the overall preference of voters. In a democracy, perception matters as much as procedure, and any gap between the popular vote and the official outcome can appear unfair.

Critics also say the system discourages participation in certain places. Voters in states that strongly favor one party may feel their individual vote has little effect on the presidential outcome. This can create frustration and reduce the sense that every ballot matters equally. Supporters of reform often argue that a direct popular vote would give citizens in all parts of the country a stronger reason to participate, since every vote would contribute to one national total.

There is also concern that the system gives extra influence to smaller states or to state boundaries that no longer reflect modern political life. People do not experience national issues only through their state identity, critics say, yet the electoral structure treats states as the key units of political value. This can seem outdated in a country where communication, travel, and economic life are deeply interconnected.

In the end, criticism of the presidential electoral voting system is rooted in the belief that leadership in a democracy should rest on the clearest and most equal expression of the people’s will. For opponents, any system that can distort that will, even indirectly, deserves serious reconsideration.

In East Germany, cross-border contact and emigration were deeply connected to everyday life, political control, and personal hope. The state tried to limit contact with the outside world, especially with West Germany, because such contact could weaken loyalty to the socialist system. Travel was restricted, private communication was monitored, and many people needed official permission for visits that would have been ordinary in other countries.

Even under these limits, cross-border contact never disappeared. Families were often divided by the inner-German border, so letters, parcels, and occasional visits became emotionally important. Radio and television from the West also created a form of indirect contact. People could compare lifestyles, language, consumer goods, and public debate. This did not affect everyone in the same way, but it often widened the gap between official propaganda and private opinion.

Emigration became a major issue because many East Germans wanted more freedom of movement, better economic opportunities, or reunion with relatives. Leaving the country without permission was treated as a serious offense, so legal emigration was difficult and often slow. Those who applied to leave could face pressure at work, social disadvantages, or suspicion from authorities. At the same time, the wish to emigrate showed that many citizens did not fully accept the limits placed on their lives.

Cross-border contact could encourage the desire to leave, but it could also strengthen emotional ties and a sense of shared identity across the border. For some, contact offered comfort rather than escape. For others, it made staying harder.

In this way, cross-border contact and emigration reveal a central tension in East Germany: the state aimed to control movement, information, and loyalty, while many individuals continued to seek connection, choice, and personal freedom.

Recurrent neural networks can be useful for modeling retinal neural responses because the retina processes visual input over time, not just frame by frame. Light patterns change continuously, and retinal neurons often depend on recent stimulation as well as the current image. A recurrent model is designed to capture this temporal context by feeding information from earlier moments back into later computations.

In this setting, the input to the model is usually a time-varying visual stimulus, while the output is the predicted activity of one or more retinal neurons. The recurrent structure allows the model to represent effects such as adaptation, delayed responses, and sensitivity to motion or temporal contrast. These are difficult to describe with purely static models that treat each moment independently.

A typical approach combines spatial and temporal processing. Early layers may extract visual features from the stimulus, while recurrent units summarize how those features evolve over time. The model then maps this internal state to neural firing rates or spike probabilities. By learning from recorded responses, the network can adjust its parameters so that its predictions better match observed retinal activity.

One advantage of recurrent models is flexibility. They can approximate complex response patterns without requiring a hand-built description of every retinal mechanism. At the same time, this flexibility creates challenges. Such models may be harder to interpret biologically, may require substantial training data, and can overfit if not carefully regularized.

Even with these limitations, recurrent neural networks offer a valuable framework for linking dynamic visual input to retinal output. They help researchers study how temporal information is encoded and can support both prediction and hypothesis generation in computational neuroscience.

While the distribution of comparatively small amplitudes can be described approximately by the universal Porter–Thomas formulas familiar from random matrix theory, the behavior of large amplitudes is significantly altered by localization effects. In particular, we identify multifractal behavior of eigenstates in 2D conductors, arising from the non-integer power-law scaling of the inverse participation numbers (IPN) with system size. This finding holds for all fundamental symmetry classes, namely unitary, orthogonal, and symplectic. In short quasi-1D wires, the pre-localized states also exhibit power-law tails, $|\psi (x)|^2\propto x^{-2}$, although their IPNs do not suggest fractal behavior. Using a saddle-point treatment of a reduced supersymmetric \(\sigma\)-model, we calculate the distribution function for local amplitudes of single-particle states in disordered conductors. For comparatively small amplitudes, this distribution is well approximated by the universal Porter-Thomas expressions familiar from random matrix theory. By contrast, localization effects substantially alter the statistics in the large-amplitude regime. In 2D conductors, specifically, we obtain multifractal eigenstate behavior, reflected in the non-integer power-law scaling of the inverse participation numbers (IPN) with system size. This conclusion applies across all fundamental symmetry classes: unitary, orthogonal, and symplectic.  

The origin of this multifractality is the presence of pre-localized states, whose wave-function envelopes decay as a power law, \( |\psi_t(r)|^2 \propto r^{-2\mu} \), with \(\mu < 1\). Short quasi-1D wires also exhibit pre-localized states with similar power-law tails, \( |\psi(x)|^2 \propto x^{-2} \), although in that case the IPN do not signal any fractal behavior. Finally, for the most extreme wave-function amplitude fluctuations in 2D and 3D conductors, the distribution function shows logarithmically normal asymptotic behavior.

In a disordered conductor, electrons do not move through a perfectly regular landscape. Instead, they encounter random variations that scatter their wavefunctions and reshape how probability is distributed in space. Wavefunction amplitude statistics describe this distribution: they ask how often the amplitude is small, typical, or unusually large at different points in a sample.

These statistics are important because they reveal more than average transport properties. In weak disorder, amplitudes may fluctuate around values expected for extended states, with only modest spatial variation. As disorder grows, rare peaks become more significant, indicating that the wavefunction is concentrating in limited regions. This behavior is closely related to interference, since multiple scattered paths can reinforce or cancel one another.

Near a localization transition, amplitude statistics become especially broad and irregular. Simple Gaussian intuition often fails, and one must consider strong fluctuations and rare events. The resulting patterns are linked to conductance variability, sensitivity to boundaries, and the distinction between metallic and localized regimes. For this reason, amplitude statistics provide a useful window into the microscopic structure of quantum states in disordered systems.

What once looked like a carved face appeared more clearly as an ordinary landform shaped by geology, shadow, and viewing angle. It shows how limited visual information can encourage bold interpretations, and how better observations can test them. In the early age of modern skyscrapers, some designers imagined that very tall buildings could do more than provide offices and observation decks. They also pictured them as vertical transport hubs, where airships might arrive high above the crowded streets. In this vision, a skyscraper would include a mooring point near its top, allowing a lighter-than-air craft to dock directly with the building.

The idea was attractive for several reasons. Airships were associated with elegance, long-distance travel, and a futuristic style of movement. Bringing them to the upper levels of a tower seemed to match the ambition of cities that wanted to present themselves as symbols of progress. A passenger might, in theory, step off an airship and enter the building without needing a separate ground terminal far away.

However, the concept faced obvious practical difficulties. Winds become stronger and less predictable at great height, and a large airship is highly sensitive to air currents. Safe docking would require careful control, specialized equipment, and ideal weather conditions. The motion of the craft, combined with the limited space around a tower, would make routine operations difficult and potentially dangerous.

For these reasons, the planned use of a skyscraper as an airship docking point remained more a striking architectural dream than a practical transportation system. Even so, the concept still captures the imagination as a symbol of bold urban optimism and technological ambition.

We employ the Gamow shell model (GSM) to describe low-lying states of the oxygen isotopes 24O and 25O. The many-body Schrodinger equation is solved starting from a two-body Hamiltonian defined by a renormalized low-momentum nucleon-nucleon (NN) interaction and a spherical Berggren basis. The Berggren basis treats bound, resonant, and continuum states on an equal footing and is therefore an appropriate representation of loosely bound and unbound nuclear states near threshold. We show that such a basis is necessary in order to obtain a detailed and correct description of the low-lying 1+ and 2+ excited states in 24O. On the other hand, we find that a correct description of the binding-energy systematics of the ground states is driven by the proper treatment and inclusion of many-body correlation effects. This is supported by the fact that we find 25O to be unstable with respect to 24O in both oscillator and Berggren representations starting from a 22O core. Furthermore, we show that the structure of these loosely bound or unbound isotopes is strongly influenced by the 1S0 component of the NN interaction. This has important consequences for our understanding of nuclear stability.

Nuclear structure modeling of neutron-rich oxygen isotopes is an important topic in modern nuclear physics because these nuclei test how well theories describe systems with a large excess of neutrons. Oxygen isotopes provide a useful chain for study: as neutrons are added, the balance between shell structure, pairing, and continuum effects becomes increasingly delicate. Models must explain why some isotopes remain bound while others quickly become unstable.

A central question is how traditional shell closures change in neutron-rich environments. In these isotopes, the ordering and spacing of single-particle orbitals can shift, and correlations among nucleons may become stronger. As a result, simple mean-field pictures are often not sufficient on their own. More advanced approaches include configuration mixing, effective interactions tailored to limited model spaces, and methods that connect bound states with weakly bound or unbound motion near the particle emission threshold.

Another challenge is the role of three-body forces and the coupling to the continuum. These ingredients can strongly influence predicted energies, radii, and excitation patterns. Successful modeling therefore requires a careful treatment of both many-body correlations and the open nature of weakly bound nuclei. Overall, neutron-rich oxygen isotopes serve as a stringent benchmark for improving nuclear theory and for understanding the limits of nuclear existence.

Bullets have a lot of momentum associated with them because they are going so fast. If you stop a bullet, all that energy has to go somewhere. If the bullet slams into a bone that stops it dead, all that kinetic energy will be absorbed into the bone, and it is liable to explode and send shards throughout the body. If the bullet is stopped by soft tissue, the energy will get diffused all around and can form a cavity up to 30x larger than the bullet itself. Having a bullet go straight through you is bad because it could still hit a major blood vessel and it leaves two holes to fix, but the alternative associated with only an entry wound is frequently much worse.

The idea that the bullet needs to be removed for an infection risk is complete BS. Trauma surgeons frequently don't even remove the bullet if going after it would induce more trauma, because if the bullet is stable (not moving), it's really not going to hurt anything. The infection risk is way higher for the gaping hole than for any chunk of hot metal that is probably sterile.

If it strikes bone and is halted immediately, the bone can absorb the full force of that kinetic energy, making it likely to shatter and send fragments through the body. When soft tissue stops the bullet instead, the energy tends to spread outward, potentially creating a cavity as much as 30 times larger than the bullet itself. A through-and-through gunshot wound is still serious, since the bullet may hit a major blood vessel and leaves two wounds that need treatment, but the situation where there is only an entry wound is often far worse.

The claim that a retained bullet must be removed because of infection risk is nonsense. In many cases, trauma surgeons will leave a bullet in place if removing it would cause additional damage, because a stable bullet that is not moving usually does no harm. The much greater infection danger comes from the large open wound, not from a piece of hot metal that is likely sterile.

When a bullet stops inside the body, the damage can still be severe. The bullet transfers energy to tissue as it slows, which may tear skin, muscle, blood vessels, nerves, and organs. In some cases, the bullet changes direction after hitting bone or dense tissue, creating a less predictable wound path. Even without an exit wound, internal bleeding can be heavy and life-threatening.

A retained bullet may also increase the risk of infection, especially if clothing, dirt, or fragments are carried into the wound. Swelling and inflammation can add pressure around injured areas, sometimes reducing blood flow or affecting nearby nerves. If the bullet rests near a joint, spine, or major vessel, it can cause ongoing pain or serious complications.

However, a bullet that remains in the body is not always removed immediately. Doctors weigh the risks of surgery against the risks of leaving it in place. The overall effect depends on where the bullet traveled and what structures it damaged.

An Old Captivity is a novel by British author Nevil Shute. It was first published in the UK in 1940 by William Heinemann.

Plot summary

The principal character is a young Scottish pilot with bush-flying experience in Canada, Donald Ross, who is hired by an Oxford don, Cyril Lockwood, to pilot an air survey mission of Brattalid in Greenland. Lockwood's interest is in the early Viking seafarers and their exploits, and although he appears to have little knowledge of the needs of such a project, he insists on their starting as soon as possible, with his elder brother David, a businessman, providing finance.

Ross, as the hired expert, then has to contend with the 'helpful' suggestions of both the financier and Lockwood's young daughter, Alix. This causes early tensions in the preparatory stages.

While the preliminary dig is ongoing, Ross shoulders much responsibility, including keeping the aircraft safe in a tidal zone. Worn out with the expedition's work – all of which has fallen solely on him – and by a prolonged lack of sleep induced by worry over the expedition, he enters a coma induced by the sleeping tablets he has been forced to take to keep going, and in it dreams that he and Alix were once Scottish slaves aboard Leif Ericson's vessel on its voyage of discovery to Greenland. A part of this dream includes the two slaves leaving behind a stone, with their names carved on it, at the Viking explorers' landing point in North America.

Ross recovers and tells Alix and the don of his dreams. The last remnant of the photographic survey is successfully completed, and the three complete their air crossing to North America, making landfall in eastern Canada. Flying down the coast towards New York, Ross recognizes where he dreamed Leif Ericson's expedition landed on the coast of Cape Cod; they land to investigate and find the stone with the slaves' names on it.

The technical details of a trans-Atlantic flight of this period (late 1930s) are accurate and of interest. The type of aircraft is a fictional radial-engined floatplane intended for bush use, made by a fictional Detroit firm named Cosmos. It corresponds roughly to the performance of a Noorduyn Norseman.

This was Shute's first attempt at re-incarnation as a plot; a second later work on this theme is In the Wet.

*Nevil Shute’s* **An Old Captivity** is a British novel, originally issued in the United Kingdom in 1940 by William Heinemann.

**Plot summary**

The story centers on Donald Ross, a young Scottish pilot who has gained bush-flying experience in Canada. He is recruited by Cyril Lockwood, an Oxford academic, to fly an aerial survey expedition to Brattalid in Greenland. Lockwood is fascinated by the early Viking voyagers and their achievements, and despite seeming to know little about the practical demands of such an undertaking, he is determined to begin without delay. Financial backing comes from his older brother David, a businessman.

As the professional pilot, Ross soon finds himself dealing with the well-meant interference of both David and Lockwood’s daughter, Alix. Their suggestions create friction from the outset during the expedition’s preparations.

Once the initial excavation begins, Ross carries a heavy burden of responsibility, including the difficult task of protecting the aircraft in a tidal area. Exhausted by the work of the expedition, much of which has fallen entirely to him, and weakened by ongoing sleeplessness caused by anxiety, he eventually falls into a coma after taking the sleeping tablets he has relied on to continue functioning. During this state, he dreams that he and Alix had once been Scottish slaves aboard Leif Ericson’s ship during its voyage to Greenland. In the dream, the two slaves leave behind a stone at the Viking landing site in North America, carving their names into it.

After recovering, Ross recounts the dream to Alix and Lockwood. The remaining photographic survey work is then completed successfully, and the three continue by air across to North America, reaching land in eastern Canada. As Ross flies south along the coast toward New York, he realizes he is seeing the place from his dream where Leif Ericson’s party came ashore near Cape Cod. They land to examine the site and discover the stone bearing the slaves’ names.

The novel is notable for its accurate and engaging treatment of the technical aspects of a late-1930s transatlantic flight. Its aircraft is an invented bush-type floatplane with a radial engine, supposedly built by a fictional Detroit company called Cosmos. In general performance, it is roughly comparable to the Noorduyn Norseman.

This novel was Shute’s first use of reincarnation as a plot device; he returned to the same theme later in *In the Wet*.

An adventure novel about an Arctic expedition and a past-life mystery can combine physical danger with psychological suspense in a powerful way. The frozen setting offers more than dramatic scenery. It creates isolation, silence, and constant pressure, making every decision feel serious. In such a story, the landscape itself becomes an opponent: shifting ice, violent storms, long darkness, and the threat of being cut off from rescue. These elements naturally support an exciting plot, but they also deepen the emotional atmosphere.

At the center of the novel is usually a journey into two unknown worlds at once. One is the external world of snowfields, glaciers, and hidden routes across the ice. The other is an inner world shaped by memory, intuition, and the disturbing possibility that the protagonist has lived before. The mystery of a past life can begin with dreams, sudden flashes of recognition, or an unexplained familiarity with a place the character has never visited. As the expedition moves farther north, these experiences may become stronger, suggesting a connection between the present mission and an unfinished story from another existence.

This combination allows the novel to explore several themes. Survival is the most obvious one, since the Arctic demands endurance, teamwork, and courage. But identity is just as important. If the protagonist feels tied to a forgotten life, then the expedition becomes more than a scientific or exploratory mission. It turns into a search for truth about the self. The past-life element can also raise questions about fate, guilt, and whether old choices continue to shape the present.

A strong version of this kind of novel often balances action with mystery. Readers expect perilous travel, hidden clues, and moments of betrayal or doubt within the expedition group. At the same time, they want the deeper puzzle to unfold gradually. The best tension comes when natural threats and supernatural hints seem to point toward the same secret.

In the end, an Arctic adventure with a past-life mystery can be compelling because it joins harsh realism with haunting imagination. The ice preserves what has been lost, and the protagonist’s journey across it becomes a journey toward buried memory, danger, and revelation.

This paper introduces a new time-frequency representation method for biomedical signals: the dyadic aggregated autoregressive (DASAR) model. Signals such as electroencephalograms (EEGs) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) exhibit physiological information through time-evolving spectral components at specific frequency intervals: 0-50 Hz (EEG) or 0-150 mHz (fNIRS). Spectrotemporal features in signals are conventionally estimated using the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) and wavelet transform (WT). However, both methods may not offer the most robust or compact representation despite their widespread use in biomedical contexts. The presented method, DASAR, improves precise frequency identification and tracking of interpretable frequency components with a parsimonious set of parameters. DASAR achieves these characteristics by assuming that the biomedical time-varying spectrum comprises several independent stochastic oscillators with (piecewise) time-varying frequencies. Local stationarity can be assumed within dyadic subdivisions of the recordings, while the stochastic oscillators can be modeled with an aggregation of second-order autoregressive models (ASAR). DASAR can provide a more accurate representation of the (highly contrasted) EEG and fNIRS frequency ranges by increasing estimation accuracy in a user-defined spectrum region of interest (SROI). A mental arithmetic experiment on hybrid EEG-fNIRS was conducted to assess the efficiency of the method. Our proposed technique, STFT, and WT were applied to both biomedical signals to discover potential oscillators that improve discrimination between the task condition and its baseline. The results show that DASAR provided the highest spectrum differentiation, and it was the only method that could identify Mayer waves as narrow-band artifacts at 97.4-97.5 mHz.

This study presents a novel time-frequency representation approach for biomedical signals, called the dyadic aggregated autoregressive (DASAR) model. In signals such as electroencephalograms (EEGs) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), physiological information appears in spectral components that evolve over time within specific frequency bands, namely 0–50 Hz for EEG and 0–150 mHz for fNIRS. Traditionally, spectrotemporal characteristics are estimated with the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) or the wavelet transform (WT). Although these techniques are widely used in biomedical applications, they do not always provide the most compact or robust representation.

To address this limitation, DASAR is designed to improve the precise identification of frequencies and the tracking of interpretable spectral components while relying on a parsimonious parameterization. The method is based on the assumption that the time-varying biomedical spectrum is composed of several independent stochastic oscillators whose frequencies vary over time, possibly in a piecewise manner. It further assumes local stationarity within dyadic partitions of the recordings, and represents the stochastic oscillators through an aggregation of second-order autoregressive models (ASAR).

By focusing estimation more accurately within a user-defined spectrum region of interest (SROI), DASAR can better represent the highly contrasted frequency ranges of EEG and fNIRS. Its effectiveness was evaluated in a mental arithmetic experiment using hybrid EEG-fNIRS recordings. The proposed method was compared with STFT and WT on both types of biomedical signals in order to identify potential oscillators that enhance discrimination between the task condition and the baseline. The findings indicate that DASAR produced the strongest spectral differentiation, and it was also the only approach able to detect Mayer waves as narrow-band artifacts in the 97.4–97.5 mHz range.

Time-frequency modeling is a useful approach in biomedical signal analysis because many physiological signals change over time and contain information at multiple frequencies. A simple view in only the time domain may show when a signal rises or falls, while a pure frequency view may show which rhythms are present. Time-frequency methods combine these perspectives, helping researchers and clinicians examine how patterns evolve moment by moment.

This is especially important for signals that are nonstationary, meaning their properties are not constant over time. Brain activity, heart rhythms, muscle signals, and breathing patterns often include transient events, shifts in oscillatory behavior, and brief irregularities. Time-frequency modeling can reveal these changes more clearly than methods that assume a stable signal structure.

Common goals include detecting events, separating meaningful components from noise, and describing the energy distribution of a signal across time and frequency. In practice, this can support tasks such as identifying abnormal episodes, tracking physiological states, comparing healthy and altered patterns, or extracting features for automated analysis. The resulting representations may appear as maps or surfaces that highlight where important activity is concentrated.

A major challenge is balancing detail in time with detail in frequency. Very sharp timing may reduce frequency precision, while strong frequency resolution may blur short events. Biomedical data also bring practical difficulties such as artifacts, motion interference, missing segments, and large variability between individuals. For this reason, effective modeling often combines signal processing knowledge with careful preprocessing and domain understanding.

Overall, time-frequency modeling provides a flexible framework for studying complex biomedical signals. By capturing both when and at what rhythm important activity occurs, it can improve interpretation, support decision-making, and deepen insight into dynamic physiological processes.

We analyze the local field of stellar tangential velocities for a sample of $42\,339$ non-binary Hipparcos stars with accurate parallaxes, using a vector spherical harmonic formalism. We derive simple relations between the parameters of the classical linear model (Ogorodnikov-Milne) of the local systemic field and low-degree terms of the general vector harmonic decomposition. The local stellar velocity field describes how stars near the Sun move through space relative to one another and to the Galaxy as a whole. These motions are not random in a simple sense. They reflect the combined effects of Galactic rotation, the gravitational pull of the disk and halo, and the past history of star formation, scattering, and orbital evolution.

Galactic kinematics studies these motions without requiring a full model of the forces that produce them. By measuring a star’s motion across the sky, its distance, and its motion along the line of sight, astronomers can reconstruct its space velocity. When this is done for many nearby stars, patterns appear. Some stars share similar motions because they were born together or were shaped by the same dynamical processes. Others show systematic trends linked to the Sun’s own motion and to the differential rotation of the Milky Way.

The local velocity field is therefore a useful probe of Galactic structure. It helps reveal how stars orbit within the disk, how stellar populations differ by age and origin, and how non-uniform features such as spiral structure or large-scale asymmetries can influence nearby motions. It also shows that the solar neighborhood is not perfectly smooth or fully mixed.

In a broader sense, local stellar motions provide a bridge between individual stars and the Galaxy’s global behavior. By mapping these velocities carefully, astronomers gain insight into the present state of the Milky Way and the processes that have shaped it over time.

Public discussion may also push schools, workplaces, and governments to improve prevention, reporting systems, and access to care.

Survivors may face online abuse, loss of privacy, or pressure to tell their stories before they are ready. At the same time, public debate can become polarized, with people treating cases as symbols instead of listening carefully to those involved.

A healthy societal response requires empathy, due process, trauma-informed services, and education about consent. Media should inform the public while protecting dignity and avoiding stereotypes.

**Purpose:**  
Protoplasmic tubes from *Physarum polycephalum*, often referred to as Physarum Wires (PWs), have been proposed as innovative bio-electronic components. However, until recently, there have been few practical demonstrations of electronic circuits built with PWs. One important benefit of these structures is their ability to self-repair, giving them a clear advantage over conventional electronic components. This article describes efforts to develop practical circuits based on PWs.

**Method:**  
By fabricating and testing hybrid circuits, we demonstrated that PWs are capable of supporting a range of practical electronic applications. Multiple uses of PWs were examined in order to demonstrate their broad applicability in both analogue and digital electronics.

**Results:**  
Using two PWs connected in series, it is possible to create voltage dividers with output voltages accurate to within 12%. PWs were also shown to carry both analogue and digital signals at frequencies up to 19 kHz and, when combined with a buffer, they can operate high-current circuits. We further showed that PWs can remain viable for about two months, representing a fourfold improvement over earlier reports. In addition, the functionality of protoplasmic tubes can be altered through the incorporation of conductive or magnetic nanoparticles.

**Conclusion:**  
This work documents novel macro-scale data transmission through biological material and advances the field of bio-electronics by presenting a low-cost, easily grown conductive biomaterial that could be used in future hybrid electronic technologies.

Biological conductive tubes are an emerging idea for hybrid electronic circuits, where living or bio-derived structures are combined with conventional components. The basic concept is simple: a soft tubular material can guide electrical signals while also offering properties that ordinary wires do not have. Because such tubes may be flexible, self-organizing, and responsive to their surroundings, they attract interest for devices that need to operate in delicate or changing environments.

In a hybrid circuit, these conductive tubes could act as tiny pathways between sensors, processors, or actuators. Their main advantage is not only conductivity, but also compatibility with soft materials and wet conditions. This makes them appealing for wearable systems, biointerfaces, and experimental robotics. In some designs, the tube may also transport fluids or chemical signals, allowing electrical and biological functions to exist in the same structure.

At the same time, there are important challenges. Biological materials can be unstable, sensitive to temperature, moisture, and contamination, and difficult to manufacture with consistent performance. Engineers must also solve questions of durability, control, and integration with standard electronics.

Even so, biological conductive tubes suggest a future in which circuits are not just rigid assemblies, but adaptive systems that blur the boundary between technology and living matter.

This dessert is often served on its own, but it also pairs well with a scoop of ice cream or a little whipped cream. Overall, caramel-topped brownies are a simple yet indulgent dessert that highlights the appeal of chocolate and caramel together.

The nontrivial zeros of the zeta function lie at the center of one of the deepest questions in mathematics. These zeros are complex numbers where the function becomes zero, excluding the more obvious negative even integers. What makes them important is their close connection to the distribution of prime numbers. The way primes appear among the integers is irregular, yet the zeros seem to encode that irregularity in a precise analytic form.

All known nontrivial zeros lie inside a vertical strip of the complex plane, and evidence strongly suggests that they all sit on a single central line within that strip. This expectation is the famous hypothesis that guides much of the subject. If true, it would sharpen many results about how regularly primes are distributed.

The zeros do not appear randomly. They show patterns in spacing and symmetry, but these patterns are subtle and still not fully understood. Mathematicians study them through analysis, computation, and comparisons with models from other areas. The overall picture is one of hidden order: a sequence that looks mysterious at first, yet seems governed by deep structure.

I took a tour of the Nevada Test Site where, until 1991, when the non-nuclear testing treaty was signed with Russia, they tested all US nuclear weapons. Over 800 underground tests were performed there. How it works is they dig an extremely deep tunnel, 5,000 ft or more; they then build a vessel to drop down the tunnel which contains the nuclear weapon, and above it, several testing instruments. The vessel is then dropped down the hole with a stream of wires from the testing instruments to the surface. The hole is then sealed, and the bomb is detonated, vaporizing everything within a radius of the bomb's blasting power (including the testing instruments). A cavity is formed by the vaporization, and eventually the earth sinks to fill it in, leaving a crater at surface level.  
The reason for testing underground is probably obvious: it does not leave radioactive material exposed to humans.

The process worked like this: they dug a very deep shaft, often 5,000 feet or more, then built a container that was lowered into the shaft holding the nuclear weapon, with several testing instruments placed above it. The container was sent down the hole along with a bundle of wires connecting the instruments to the surface. The shaft was then sealed, and the bomb was detonated, vaporizing everything within the range of the blast, including the testing instruments. This created a cavity, and over time the ground collapsed into it, leaving a crater on the surface.

The reason for conducting the tests underground is fairly obvious: it prevented radioactive material from being left exposed to people.

Underground nuclear weapons testing site operations involve a tightly controlled sequence of technical, safety, and security activities. The main goal is to contain the explosive event deep below the surface while collecting data on weapon performance and the behavior of surrounding rock and soil.

Before any test, specialists study local geology to choose a location with stable underground formations. Engineers then design a shaft or tunnel system that can hold the device and support monitoring equipment. Instruments are placed to measure pressure, heat, ground motion, radiation, and other effects. Cables and sensors must be protected so they can transmit information during the brief moment of detonation.

Containment is a central concern. The device is sealed in a deep emplacement area, and the access route is backfilled with layers of material intended to reduce the chance of radioactive gases reaching the surface. Security teams restrict access, while emergency crews prepare for possible accidents during handling, transport, or setup.

During the test, operations are coordinated from a remote control point. Staff follow strict procedures, verify communications, and monitor environmental conditions. After detonation, teams assess whether the explosion remained contained. They examine seismic signals, inspect the ground for subsidence or venting, and review instrument data.

Long after the event, the site may require continued monitoring, cleanup, and access controls. Even when no visible damage appears at the surface, underground testing can leave lasting environmental and political consequences.

We perform a detailed study of inverse Compton (IC) emission for a fireball undergoing external shock (ES) in either a uniform or a wind-like interstellar medium, and assess the relative importance of IC and synchrotron emissions. We determine the primary model parameters driving the IC-to-synchrotron emission ratio in the case of a short-duration central engine. We then investigate the case of ES by a long-duration central engine, or delayed external shock (DES), a model that can account for some of the flares observed in GRB X-ray light curves. We present model predictions, in particular in terms of GeV vs. X-ray behavior, and compare them with other models proposed to explain the origin of flares. We find that if most of the emission occurs when the fireball is in the fast-cooling regime, then a substantial GeV emission is expected both for a short (standard ES) and a long (DES) duration of central engine activity. In particular, in the context of standard ES we are able to account for the delayed emission observed in GRB940217. In the case of DES, we find that IC scattering of X-ray flare photons can produce high-energy flares in the GeV band, which can be detected by GLAST. The detectability of high-energy flares improves with the burst kinetic energy: about 30% of Swift GRBs showing flares in their X-ray light curve have sufficiently large kinetic energy so that the expected high-energy flares can be detected by GLAST. One important prediction of the DES model is the simultaneity between low- and high-energy flares. To test this simultaneity, the peak energies of both flares need to fall below or within the observational bands. We predict that X-ray flares with peak energy of ~10 eV produce high-energy flares with peak energy of around 100 MeV-GeV. Observations by Swift and GLAST, then, can test the predicted simultaneity.

High-energy emission in gamma-ray burst shock models is usually explained as radiation produced when an ultra-fast outflow dissipates part of its energy in shocks. In these models, the burst begins with a relativistic jet launched by a compact central engine. Because different parts of the flow can move at different speeds, faster shells may catch slower ones and create internal shocks. Later, as the jet plows into the surrounding medium, an external shock forms and drives a blast wave outward.

Both kinds of shocks can accelerate electrons to very high energies and amplify magnetic fields. The simplest radiation process is synchrotron emission, in which energetic electrons spiral in magnetic fields and emit photons across a broad range of frequencies. This mechanism can account for much of the prompt and afterglow radiation, although the highest-energy photons may require additional channels. One important possibility is inverse Compton scattering, where the same electrons transfer energy to lower-energy photons and boost them into the gamma-ray band. In some cases, repeated scattering or emission from protons and secondary particles may also contribute.

The observed high-energy signal depends on several linked factors: the strength of the magnetic field, the efficiency of particle acceleration, the density of the external environment, and the bulk Lorentz factor of the outflow. Cooling is also crucial. Electrons can lose energy rapidly, which shapes the spectrum and the timing of the emission. At very high energies, photon-photon absorption may suppress part of the signal before it escapes, while interactions during propagation can further reduce the flux.

Shock models are attractive because they connect radiation with the dynamics of the outflow and naturally predict evolving spectra and light curves. At the same time, they face challenges, especially in explaining very hard spectra, extreme radiative efficiency, and delayed high-energy components in some bursts. As a result, high-energy emission in gamma-ray bursts is often studied with hybrid pictures that combine shocks with other dissipation processes.

To understand why that is needed, you need to look at the structure of the federal government. In the United States, the Constitution gives Congress only "enumerated" powers. This means that, unlike the states, Congress is only empowered to pass laws on specific kinds of subjects.  
So, for instance, Congress can pass a law regulating interstate commerce, or pass laws to set the rules for bankruptcy. But it can't necessarily pass a law that forces everyone to exercise every day (which a state arguably could pass).

The Necessary and Proper Clause is a part of the Constitution that gives Congress the authority to pass laws needed to carry out its other powers in practice.

To see why this is important, it helps to look at the structure of the federal government. In the United States, the Constitution grants Congress only “enumerated” powers. That means that, unlike the states, Congress can make laws only on certain specified subjects.

For example, Congress can pass laws regulating interstate commerce or establish rules for bankruptcy. But it cannot necessarily pass a law requiring everyone to exercise every day, which a state could arguably do.

However, the people who wrote the Constitution were concerned that this idea might be taken too far. Congress had the power to regulate interstate commerce, but did that also include the authority to pass a law paying the salary of someone who enforces that law? If Congress has the power to regulate bankruptcy, does that also include the power to hire judges to decide bankruptcy cases?

The Necessary and Proper Clause answered that question. It gives Congress the power to pass laws that are “necessary and proper” for carrying out its other powers.

The Necessary and Proper Clause is a constitutional provision that authorizes Congress to make laws required to put its other powers into effect.

To see why this matters, it helps to consider how the federal government is organized. Under the Constitution, Congress has only enumerated powers. In other words, unlike state governments, it may legislate only in certain defined areas.

For example, Congress may regulate interstate commerce and establish rules governing bankruptcy. However, it could not simply enact a law requiring everyone to exercise every day, even though a state arguably could.

The framers of the Constitution, however, were concerned that this system might be applied too narrowly. If Congress has the authority to regulate interstate commerce, does that also allow it to pass a law paying the salary of a person who enforces that regulation? If it has the power to regulate bankruptcy, does that include the authority to hire judges to decide bankruptcy cases?

The Necessary and Proper Clause addresses that issue by giving Congress the power to enact laws that are “necessary and proper” for carrying out its other constitutional powers.

A constitutional clause enabling implied congressional powers is often understood as the provision that allows the national legislature to pass laws needed to carry out its listed responsibilities. Rather than limiting Congress only to powers stated in exact words, this clause gives practical flexibility. It recognizes that governing requires tools, procedures, and supporting measures that may not be spelled out one by one.

This idea does not create unlimited authority. The clause is usually read together with the powers specifically granted elsewhere in the constitution. In that sense, it serves as a bridge between broad constitutional goals and the everyday laws required to achieve them. It helps Congress organize institutions, enforce national policy, and respond to new problems that arise over time.

At the same time, debate often surrounds its meaning. Supporters see it as essential for effective government, while critics worry it can expand federal power too far. Its importance lies in balancing workable governance with constitutional limits.

"Merle Lindsay Salathiel (1916 – October 12, 1965), better known as Merl Lindsay, was one of the premier American Western swing musicians from the 1930s to the mid-1960s and the founder of Merl Lindsay and His Oklahoma Night Riders.

Life and career  
Merle Lindsay Salathiel was born in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, to Clarence Earl and Louella Salathiel, early pioneers of the Oklahoma Territory. He began his music career in 1936, playing fiddle in his father (C.E. Salathiel)'s ballroom, Salathiel's Barn. In 1937, he formed his first band, the Barnyard Boys. In 1947, he created a larger band and added a female singer, calling the group Merl Lindsay and His Oklahoma Night Riders. During the 1940s, he owned a ballroom in Compton, California, and broadcast over a four-station radio hookup in Hollywood and Long Beach. He also performed with Jimmy Wakely in Western B-movies.

In 1957, Lindsay joined ABC-TV's Ozark Jubilee, taking over the ten-piece Ozark Jubilee Band. His group adopted the name when the TV program's title was changed to Country Music Jubilee the next year. During his later years, he toured the US and performed at his ballroom, Lindsayland, in Oklahoma City.

Many famous Western swing musicians performed with Lindsay's bands over the years. Two of his female singers were Wanda Jackson and Norma Jean. His brother, Doyle Salathiel (1920–1976), played with Lindsay's bands as well as others, and was a composer who wrote the words for the band's signature song, "Water Baby Blues." Lindsay's nephew, Max Salathiel (1935–2006), an accomplished Oklahoma City guitar player, also worked with his band in the 1950s, as did his sister Alojah Salathiel.

Other band members included Robert "Buddy" Ray, Rudy Martin, Frederick "Freddie" Loveland, Louvenie Loveland, Ted Haff, Mike Hugo, Clarence Bailey, Homer Bean, Gerald "Buster" Magness, Gene Jones (steel guitar), and Sonny Rogers.

Lindsay was married to Doris Salathiel. He had three children, Merlynn Salathiel, Denzel Salathiel (1952-2016), and Jackie Merle Phillips (1934-2000). Lindsay died in Oklahoma City from cancer on October 12, 1965. He is buried in Sunnylane Cemetery in Del City, Oklahoma.

Compositions  
Lindsay wrote many songs that became hits for himself and other Western swing artists. Among them:  
"Lonesome Okie Goin' Home"  
"Shimmy Shakin' Daddy"  
"Slidin' Steel" (with Gene Crownover)  
"Water Baby Blues/Water Baby Boogie"

## Life and career

Merle Lindsay Salathiel was born in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, to Clarence Earl and Louella Salathiel, who were among the early pioneers of the Oklahoma Territory. He launched his musical career in 1936, playing fiddle at his father C.E. Salathiel’s ballroom, Salathiel’s Barn. A year later, in 1937, he organized his first group, the Barnyard Boys.

In 1947, Lindsay expanded his musical ambitions by forming a larger ensemble and including a female vocalist. He named this new band Merl Lindsay and His Oklahoma Night Riders. During the 1940s, he also owned a ballroom in Compton, California, and his performances were carried on a four-station radio network serving Hollywood and Long Beach. In addition, he appeared with Jimmy Wakely in Western B-movies.

A major change came in 1957, when Lindsay joined ABC-TV’s *Ozark Jubilee* and assumed leadership of the ten-piece Ozark Jubilee Band. When the television show was retitled *Country Music Jubilee* the following year, his band adopted that name as well. In his later years, he toured across the United States and continued performing at his own Oklahoma City ballroom, Lindsayland.

Over time, Lindsay’s bands featured many notable Western swing musicians. Among the female singers who worked with him were Wanda Jackson and Norma Jean. His brother, Doyle Salathiel (1920–1976), performed not only with Lindsay’s groups but with others as well, and he wrote the lyrics to the band’s signature song, “Water Baby Blues.” Lindsay’s nephew, Max Salathiel (1935–2006), a respected Oklahoma City guitarist, also played with the band during the 1950s, as did Lindsay’s sister, Alojah Salathiel.

Other musicians associated with his bands included Robert “Buddy” Ray, Rudy Martin, Frederick “Freddie” Loveland, Louvenie Loveland, Ted Haff, Mike Hugo, Clarence Bailey, Homer Bean, Gerald “Buster” Magness, Gene Jones on steel guitar, and Sonny Rogers.

Lindsay was married to Doris Salathiel. His children were Merlynn Salathiel, Denzel Salathiel (1952–2016), and Jackie Merle Phillips (1934–2000). He died of cancer in Oklahoma City on October 12, 1965, and was buried at Sunnylane Cemetery in Del City, Oklahoma.

A western swing bandleader and fiddler often stands at the crossroads of several musical worlds. His life story usually begins in a rural setting where dance music, church songs, cowboy ballads, and fiddle tunes all mix together. From an early age, he is drawn to the sound of the violin, not as a formal concert instrument, but as a lively voice for community gatherings. He learns by listening, imitating older players, and absorbing melodies that travel from front porches to barn dances and radio programs.

As he grows into a performer, the fiddler becomes more than a solo musician. He develops the instincts of a bandleader, learning how to shape a group sound that keeps dancers moving while still giving each player room to shine. Western swing depends on this balance. It blends string band traditions with the rhythmic drive of jazz, the plainspoken feeling of country music, and the easy charm of popular song. The bandleader’s fiddle remains central, but it no longer works alone. It trades phrases with guitars, steel guitar, piano, horns, and drums, creating a style that feels both rooted and adventurous.

What sets such a musician apart is often his ability to unite audiences. He can play a sentimental waltz with warmth and restraint, then turn to an upbeat number full of swing rhythm and playful improvisation. As a frontman, he must also read the room, pace a set, and keep the ensemble tight. His leadership is heard not only in solos but in arrangements, introductions, endings, and the overall mood of a performance. He understands that western swing is social music: it is meant for dancing, celebration, and shared pleasure.

Over time, the bandleader and fiddler may become a symbol of a regional sound. He helps carry local traditions into a broader public space through touring, broadcasts, recordings, and dance halls. In doing so, he preserves older fiddle styles while also modernizing them. This dual role is important. Western swing thrives on respect for tradition, yet it also welcomes experimentation, syncopation, and instrumental conversation borrowed from other genres.

The legacy of a western swing bandleader and fiddler lies in that spirit of connection. He links rural and urban audiences, old melodies and new rhythms, disciplined ensemble playing and spontaneous invention. Even when musical fashions change, his influence can remain strong because the style he represents is flexible and joyful. Later musicians continue to study his bowing, timing, phrasing, and leadership, not simply to copy them, but to understand how one performer could turn regional dance music into a rich, durable art form.

High top tax rates can influence investment in several ways, and their effects are often debated. One common argument is that higher taxes on top earners may reduce the amount of private capital available for new business ventures, expansion, or risk-taking. If investors expect a smaller share of future returns, they may become more cautious about funding uncertain projects, especially those with long time horizons.

At the same time, the effect is not always simple or direct. Many investment decisions depend on broader conditions such as demand, interest rates, business confidence, and access to credit. A profitable opportunity may still attract funding even when tax rates are high. In addition, some investors focus on long-term stability more than on short-term tax burdens.

High top tax rates can also affect how money is used rather than whether it is invested at all. Individuals and firms may shift resources toward tax planning, safer assets, or forms of compensation that receive different treatment. This can change the pattern of investment across sectors.

On the other hand, if higher tax revenue is used effectively, it may support public goods that encourage investment, such as infrastructure, education, and legal stability. In that sense, the overall impact depends not only on the tax rate itself but also on the wider economic environment and government policy. The relationship is therefore complex, with possible negative, neutral, or even positive effects depending on context.

Driven by the coupled behavior of electron charge, spin, and orbital degrees of freedom, spin-orbit torque (SOT) has become a major focus of research over the last decade. Although substantial advances have been made, current methods for quantifying SOT still face important limitations, including constraints related to magnetic anisotropy, the mixing of different SOT effective fields, and artifacts caused by thermal gradients and the planar Hall effect. As a result, there remains a pressing need for an accurate approach that can characterize SOT reliably across a wide range of samples.

A universal measurement method for spin-orbit torque aims to provide one consistent way to evaluate how electric current can control magnetization in a wide range of materials and device structures. Spin-orbit torque appears when the motion of electrons, combined with spin-orbit coupling, generates an effective torque on a magnetic layer. This effect is important because it offers a path toward fast and energy-efficient control of magnetic states in modern spintronic devices.

The challenge is that spin-orbit torque can be measured in several different ways, and each technique may emphasize different physical contributions. Results can therefore depend on sample geometry, interface quality, magnetic anisotropy, or the details of the analysis. A universal method seeks to reduce these ambiguities by using a framework that can be applied across many systems and that separates the main torque components in a reliable manner.

In practice, such a method should connect electrical signals to the underlying damping-like and field-like torques with minimal assumptions. It should work for thin films, multilayers, and patterned devices, and remain valid even when the magnetic response is complex. A strong universal approach also includes careful calibration of current, magnetic field, and thermal effects, since heating and parasitic voltages can imitate or distort the true torque signal.

The value of a universal measurement method is not only technical but also conceptual. It allows researchers to compare materials on equal terms, identify the mechanisms responsible for torque generation, and guide device optimization more efficiently. By establishing a common standard for measurement and interpretation, this approach supports clearer communication between experiments and theory and helps accelerate progress in spin-orbit torque research and applications.

Ontology-informed embeddings offer a promising way to improve medical code prediction by combining data-driven learning with structured clinical knowledge. In many healthcare tasks, a model must assign diagnosis, procedure, or billing codes to patient records. This is difficult because clinical language is varied, incomplete, and often ambiguous. Standard embeddings can capture patterns in text and records, but they may miss important relationships between codes, symptoms, findings, and broader disease categories.

An ontology provides an organized representation of medical concepts and their connections. It can describe hierarchies, synonyms, related conditions, and links between observations and interventions. When this structure is used to shape embeddings, the model can place medically related concepts closer together in the representation space. As a result, it may better recognize that different terms can point to the same condition, or that a specific code belongs within a larger diagnostic family.

This approach can support prediction in several ways. It may improve performance for rare codes by borrowing information from nearby concepts in the ontology. It can also help with generalization when training data are limited or unevenly distributed. In addition, ontology-informed embeddings may make model behavior easier to interpret, since predicted codes can be traced back to meaningful conceptual relationships rather than only to surface text patterns.

However, the method also brings challenges. Medical ontologies can be incomplete, inconsistent across settings, or slow to reflect current practice. Integrating symbolic knowledge with neural models requires careful design so that the ontology guides learning without forcing overly rigid assumptions. There is also a need to handle uncertainty, overlapping categories, and local documentation habits.

Overall, ontology-informed embeddings represent a useful middle ground between pure statistical prediction and expert-curated knowledge. By aligning learned representations with medical structure, they can make code prediction more accurate, robust, and clinically coherent.

It combines strength, timing, balance, and trust. Each person in the group has a clear role. Bases provide power and stability, the back spot helps guide the stunt and protects the flyer’s center line, and the flyer maintains body control while hitting clean positions in the air.

The sequence usually begins with a set, where the group establishes grips, posture, and timing. A smooth dip and drive from the bases creates upward force, while the flyer stays tight through the core to rise efficiently. Once the stunt reaches the intended level, the group focuses on steadiness. Small adjustments in hand placement, shoulder alignment, and weight distribution help keep the position secure.

When people face an important decision, they often feel pressure to choose quickly and confidently. However, many choices become clearer when discussed with trusted people. Seeking advice does not mean giving up independence. Instead, it can be a thoughtful way to test ideas, notice risks, and understand personal priorities more deeply.

Trusted people can offer something that is hard to create alone: perspective. When someone is emotionally involved in a problem, it is easy to focus on one fear or one hope and ignore other factors. A calm listener may ask simple but useful questions: What matters most here? What are you afraid of losing? What would happen if you waited? These questions can reveal hidden assumptions and help organize confused thoughts. In many cases, the value of advice is not only in the answer given, but in the conversation itself.

Another benefit of asking for guidance is that different people see different parts of a situation. A close friend may understand your personality and values. A family member may notice practical concerns. A mentor or experienced colleague may recognize patterns from similar situations. By hearing more than one viewpoint, a person can compare opinions and avoid relying on a single emotional reaction. This does not guarantee a perfect decision, but it often leads to a more balanced one.

At the same time, not every opinion should carry equal weight. The best advice usually comes from people who are honest, caring, and able to listen without trying to control the outcome. Trust is important because advice can strongly influence confidence. If someone gives judgment instead of support, their words may create more confusion than clarity. For that reason, it helps to choose advisors carefully and to notice whether their guidance fits your values rather than their own preferences.

In the end, decisions still belong to the person making them. Advice should inform, not replace, personal responsibility. Listening to trusted people can reduce isolation and widen understanding, but the final choice must feel true to one’s own judgment. A wise decision is often not made alone, yet it is still made from within.

Evaluating the score of a chess position can be very challenging. Counting the pieces is a useful starting point, but there are cases where a player has fewer pieces and still holds the advantage.  
Position matters as well, since some pieces become much more effective when placed on certain squares. To handle this, a computer likely uses, for each piece type, a table that assigns different values based on its location.

That is only the simple part: to really judge how strong a position is, you also have to consider what your opponent might do on the next move, what you might do in response, and so on.  
The “perfect” algorithm would examine every possible continuation from the current position and then assign a score based on how many of those outcomes lead to a win. However, this is extremely expensive computationally, because the number of possible lines increases exponentially as the search continues.

Most engines therefore restrict themselves to looking ahead only a few moves (around 5–6) and base their evaluation on that. They consider all possible outcomes over those few turns, score them using a simple heuristic (such as piece count adjusted by position), and then return an average score or something along those lines.  
[Edit] Another method is the [monte-carlo method](_URL_0_): the computer begins from the current position and plays random moves until the game ends. It then repeats this process thousands (or millions) of times and uses the ratio of wins to losses to estimate the value of the position.

This works well as a fast heuristic and is often combined with other methods to give a better sense of the long-term game. Typically, an engine may analyze the next 5 turns more carefully and then switch to monte-carlo simulations to carry the game through to the end.

Evaluating a chess position is often very hard. A basic method is to count the material on the board, but that alone is not enough, since a player can be down in pieces and still be in a better position.

Another important element is piece placement. Certain pieces become much stronger or weaker depending on where they stand, so a computer likely uses, for each piece type, a table that assigns different values to different squares.

But that is only the easy part. To really judge how favorable a position is, you also need to consider your opponent’s next move, then your reply, then their response, and so on.

In theory, the ideal algorithm would examine every possible continuation from the current position and score the board according to how many of those continuations lead to a win. The problem is that this is enormously expensive computationally, because the number of possible lines increases exponentially the deeper the simulation goes.

For that reason, most chess engines only search a limited number of turns ahead, perhaps 5 or 6, and base their evaluation on those results. In practice, they examine all possible outcomes within that depth, score the resulting positions with a simple heuristic such as material adjusted by positional value, and then return an average score or something along those lines.

[Edit] A different method is the [monte-carlo method](_URL_0_). Starting from the current position, the computer plays random moves until the game ends, then repeats the process thousands or even millions of times. It then estimates the value of the board from the proportion of games won and lost.

This provides a strong quick heuristic and is often combined with other methods to give a better sense of the long-term position. For example, an engine might analyze the next 5 turns more carefully, then switch to monte-carlo simulations to carry the game through to the end.

Evaluating a chess position means judging which side stands better and why. Strong evaluation combines concrete calculation with general positional principles. A player does not only ask, “What can happen next?” but also, “Which side has the healthier structure and the better long-term chances?”

One common method is material assessment. Players compare the value of pieces and pawns to see whether one side has an advantage. Material alone, however, is rarely enough. A side with fewer pieces may still have compensation through activity, initiative, or attacking chances.

Another important method is examining king safety. Exposed kings, weak pawn shields, and open lines near the king often create urgent tactical possibilities. Closely related is piece activity. Well-placed pieces control key squares, cooperate with each other, and create threats. Poorly placed pieces may be blocked, passive, or disconnected from the rest of the army.

Pawn structure is also central to evaluation. Doubled, isolated, or backward pawns can become long-term weaknesses, while connected pawns and passed pawns may provide strength. Space matters as well: the side controlling more territory often has greater freedom to maneuver.

Players also consider time and initiative. A position may favor the side that can make threats faster, even if other factors look balanced. Finally, evaluation must match the phase of the game. In the opening, development matters greatly; in the endgame, king activity and pawn promotion chances become more important. Good evaluation is therefore a balance of static features and dynamic possibilities.

Public perceptions of celiac disease are often shaped by general discussions about gluten-free eating rather than by a clear understanding of the condition itself. Many people see it as a dietary preference, a mild intolerance, or part of a broader wellness trend. As a result, the seriousness of celiac disease can be overlooked. It is not simply a matter of avoiding certain foods to feel a little better; for those who have it, eating gluten can trigger an immune reaction that harms the body.

Self-diagnosis is common because the symptoms can be vague, varied, and easy to confuse with other problems. Some people experience digestive discomfort, while others notice fatigue, skin issues, headaches, or trouble concentrating. Because these signs are not unique to celiac disease, individuals may assume they have the condition after reading about it or hearing others discuss gluten sensitivity. In response, they may remove gluten from their diet without medical guidance.

This can create several problems. A person may feel temporary improvement for reasons unrelated to celiac disease, leading to false confidence in a self-diagnosis. Others may overlook a different medical issue that needs attention. In addition, starting a gluten-free diet before proper testing can make diagnosis more difficult later.

Public understanding would benefit from a more balanced view. It is helpful to recognize that celiac disease is a real medical condition, but also that symptoms alone are not enough to confirm it. Professional evaluation is important for distinguishing celiac disease from other digestive or immune-related concerns. Better awareness can reduce confusion, discourage casual assumptions, and support people in seeking accurate diagnosis and appropriate care.

History  
Harold Park is the north-eastern part of Harold Wood, occupying an isthmus of land between the A12 and the Ingrebourne River (The River Ingrebourne at Harold Park and Hornchurch).

In 1868 a wealthy Brentwood solicitor built himself a mansion to the south of the river and railway line, named Harold Court. After the owner's bankruptcy, the house served as a children's home, then a lunatic asylum, and then a sanatorium. In 1959 it became a teacher training college and has now been converted into private flats.
 
Horse Block Farm lay to the north-east of Harold Court Road. After the First World War the Essex builders Iles and Company laid out a bungalow estate here that it called Sunnytown. The company also created Sunnymede at Billericay.
 
When Harold Court Primary School opened in 1929, the area still retained a rural character, but this was slowly eroded as further development plugged the gaps, including some industry beside the Ingrebourne River.

Harold Park sits in the Parliamentary Constituency of Hornchurch and Upminster.

Harold Park sits on the London/Essex border. The boundary goes down the Weald Brook. A suburban district is often understood as the space between a busy city center and the open countryside. It usually combines residential streets, local shops, schools, parks, and transport links that connect daily life to the wider urban area. For many people, such a district represents balance: it is quieter than the inner city, yet still close enough to workplaces, services, and cultural life.

The history of a suburban district often begins with a small rural settlement or a cluster of farms on the edge of a town. As the nearby city grows, roads improve and public transport expands, making the outer area easier to reach. Over time, fields may give way to housing, small commercial streets, and community buildings. What was once a separate village can gradually become part of a larger urban region while still keeping traces of its earlier character.

In many cases, the first major period of growth comes when families seek more space, cleaner air, and a calmer environment than the crowded center can offer. New homes are built, followed by schools, medical services, and recreational spaces. Later, the district may continue to change through redevelopment, apartment construction, and the renewal of older shopping areas. At the same time, long-term residents often try to preserve green spaces, local traditions, and a sense of neighborhood identity.

Today, a suburban district is rarely just a place to sleep. It can be a lively community with its own social life, small businesses, and public spaces. Its history is usually a story of transition: from rural edge to residential expansion, and from quiet outskirts to an established part of the modern metropolitan landscape.

We analyze the microlensing event KMT-2019-BLG-0797. The light curve of the event exhibits two anomalous features relative to a single-lens single-source model, and we aim to reveal the nature of the anomaly. It is found that a model with two lenses plus a single source (2L1S model) can explain one feature of the anomaly, but the other feature cannot be explained. We test various models and find that both anomalous features can be explained by introducing an extra source to the 2L1S model (2L2S model), making the event the third confirmed case of a 2L2S event, following MOA-2010-BLG-117 and OGLE-2016-BLG-1003. It is estimated that the extra source comprises $\sim 4\%$ of the $I$-band flux from the primary source. Interpreting the event is subject to a close--wide degeneracy. According to the close solution, the lens is a binary consisting of two brown dwarfs with masses $(M_1, M_2)\sim (0.034, 0.021)~M_\odot$, and it is located at a distance of $\dl\sim 8.2$~kpc. According to the wide solution, on the other hand, the lens is composed of an object at the star/brown-dwarf boundary and an M dwarf with masses $(M_1, M_2)\sim (0.06, 0.33)~M_\odot$, located at $\dl\sim 7.7$~kpc. The source is composed of a late-G-dwarf/early-K-dwarf primary and an early-to-mid M-dwarf companion.

A gravitational microlensing anomaly event is a brief departure from the smooth brightening and fading expected when a foreground lens passes close to the line of sight to a background star. In the simplest case, a single compact lens produces a symmetric light curve whose shape depends mainly on the closest approach and the event timescale. An anomaly appears when this simple model fails to match the observations.

The analysis usually begins with careful photometry and a search for short-lived features, such as spikes, dips, or asymmetries. These features often suggest that the lens is not a single object. A binary lens, a planetary companion, or in some cases a binary source can create caustic structures that strongly amplify the source when crossed or closely approached. Because anomalies may last only a small fraction of the full event, dense time coverage is essential.

Modeling proceeds by comparing observed light curves with families of lens configurations. Parameters describing separation, mass ratio, trajectory, and source size are adjusted to reproduce the anomaly. This process is complicated by degeneracies: very different geometries can generate similar signals. Finite-source effects, parallax, and lens orbital motion may also need to be included if the data quality allows.

The final interpretation combines statistical fitting with physical plausibility. Analysts test whether the anomaly is robust against systematics, blending, and gaps in coverage. A convincing solution can reveal the presence of a companion and constrain the geometry of the lens system, even when the lens itself remains too faint to observe directly.

Seeking advice from multiple people can be very helpful when making decisions, solving problems, or planning for the future. One of the main benefits is that different people notice different things. A friend may understand your personality, a family member may know your history, and a teacher or coworker may focus on practical details. By listening to several viewpoints, you can see a situation more clearly and avoid relying on only one way of thinking.

Another advantage is that multiple opinions can reveal options you had not considered. When people come from different backgrounds or have different experiences, they often suggest new approaches. This can be especially useful when facing an unfamiliar challenge. Even if you do not follow every suggestion, hearing a range of ideas can expand your understanding and help you think more creatively.

Seeking advice from several people can also reduce the risk of poor judgment. A single person may give advice based on limited knowledge, personal bias, or emotion. If you ask others as well, you can compare their responses and look for common patterns. When several people independently point to the same concern or opportunity, that information may deserve special attention.

In addition, talking with more than one person can build confidence. Important choices often feel less overwhelming when you have taken time to gather perspectives. You may still need to make the final decision on your own, but you can do so with a stronger sense that you considered the matter carefully.

The real benefit comes from listening thoughtfully, weighing what is relevant, and choosing what fits your values and goals. Zen is a branch of Buddhism described as a mind-to-mind transmission outside the scriptures. That does not mean scriptures are rejected or unused; it means Zen is not based upon them as its foundation.

A useful image is that thoughts are like waves, while the Essence of Mind is the ocean itself. So then, what are your thoughts made of? What is their source?

A beginning point for Zen practice can be the question: “What was my original face before my parents were born?” Or, given the subreddit we’re in, before mommy and daddy were born.
